source_evidence.anchor: Introduction, definition of F and equation (1.1b)
source_evidence.observation: F is introduced as a standard radix-beta, precision-p floating-point set, with unit roundoff u = (1/2) beta^(1-p). The introduction previews the exact Cholesky backward relation and the coarse componentwise bound with constant (n+1)u.

source_evidence.anchor: equation (1.5c) and the following order-of-evaluation paragraph
source_evidence.observation: The square-root backward identity is stated under absence of underflow and overflow for any summation order. Such an order is defined through rooted binary summation trees on the input term and products.
The improved bounds are stated to hold for any radix, any tie-breaking rule, any dimension, and any evaluation order, without quadratic terms in u or a smallness restriction on the dimension.

F is a symmetric set of finite floating-point numbers with base beta >= 2, precision p >= 1, exponent range [emin, emax], and zero. The rounding map is round-to-nearest with arbitrary tie-breaking, and u = (1/2) beta^(1-p) <= 1/2. Underflow means an inexact rounding of a real number in the subnormal range.
The division specialization requires a nonzero floating-point divisor. The square-root specialization requires a nonnegative computed argument and yields the coefficient (n+1)u.
The notation diag(f(i)) denotes the n by n diagonal matrix with entry f(i) at position (i,i), with i implicitly ranging from 1 to n.

For a floating-point evaluation of a quotient of a sum, the divisor must be nonzero. In the absence of underflow and overflow, the lemma applies for any evaluation order and gives coefficient ku, reduced to (k-1)u when there is no division.

Cholesky factorization is defined as computation of the upper-triangular factor by the conventional algorithm. Lemma 4.3 treats a rounded square root of a nonnegative computed sum and gives coefficient (k+1)u for any evaluation order.

The theorem assumes only that A belongs to F^(n by n), is symmetric, the Cholesky factorization runs to completion, and no underflow or overflow occurs. It states that the computed factor Rhat belongs to F^(n by n).
The complete conclusion is Rhat^T Rhat = A + DeltaA together with |DeltaA| <= diag((i+1)u)|Rhat^T||Rhat| <= (n+1)u|Rhat^T||Rhat|.
For column j, the conventional algorithm computes off-diagonal entries from a quotient with denominator Rhat_ii and computes the diagonal entry from the square root of a diagonal residual.

The proof derives separate componentwise residual estimates with constants iu for off-diagonal entries and (j+1)u for diagonal entries, then completes the matrix result using symmetry of A - Rhat^T Rhat and Rhat^T Rhat.

binders: F is a fixed but arbitrary standard set of finite real floating-point numbers with base beta, precision p, and unit roundoff u = (1/2) beta^(1-p). [PDF p. 1 (printed 684), Introduction; PDF p. 5 (printed 688), Sections 2.1-2.2]
n is the matrix dimension, with indices running from 1 through n. [PDF p. 9 (printed 692), Section 4 notation paragraph]
A is the given symmetric matrix in F^(n by n). [PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Theorem 4.4]

Rhat is the factor in F^(n by n) produced by the successful floating-point execution of the conventional Cholesky algorithm. [PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Section 4.3 and Theorem 4.4; PDF p. 12 (printed 695), update formulas]
DeltaA is the backward perturbation introduced by the identity Rhat^T Rhat = A + DeltaA; the paper does not separately declare its scalar type. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.4)]
hypotheses: A has floating-point entries and is symmetric. [PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Theorem 4.4]
The conventional Cholesky factorization runs to completion and produces Rhat. [PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Theorem 4.4]
No underflow or overflow occurs during the relevant floating-point execution. [PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Theorem 4.4]
The inherited arithmetic model is round-to-nearest in base beta and precision p, with arbitrary tie-breaking. [PDF p. 5 (printed 688), Sections 2.1-2.2]

The inner sums may be evaluated in any order covered by the paper's binary-tree summation model. [PDF p. 3 (printed 686), paragraph following equation (1.5c); PDF p. 12 (printed 695), paragraph preceding equations (4.5a)-(4.5b)]
Positive definiteness is not a hypothesis of Theorem 4.4; the theorem replaces it by symmetry plus successful completion. [PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Section 4.3 opening and Theorem 4.4]
conclusions: The computed factor satisfies the exact backward relation Rhat^T Rhat = A + DeltaA. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.4)]
The perturbation satisfies the row-scaled componentwise bound |DeltaA| <= diag((i+1)u)|Rhat^T||Rhat|. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.4); PDF p. 9 (printed 692), diag convention]
It also satisfies the coarser componentwise bound |DeltaA| <= (n+1)u|Rhat^T||Rhat|. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.4)]
For 1 <= i <= j-1, the proof establishes |a_ij - sum_{k=1}^i Rhat_ki Rhat_kj| <= i u sum_{k=1}^i |Rhat_ki||Rhat_kj|. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.5a)]
For 1 <= j <= n, the proof establishes |a_jj - sum_{k=1}^j Rhat_kj^2| <= (j+1)u sum_{k=1}^j Rhat_kj^2. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.5b)]
DeltaA is symmetric because both A and Rhat^T Rhat are symmetric. [PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Theorem 4.4; PDF p. 12 (printed 695), closing symmetry sentence]
definitions_and_conventions: F contains finite floating-point numbers, is symmetric, and contains zero; beta >= 2 and p >= 1. [PDF p. 5 (printed 688), Section 2.1]
fl(t) is any nearest floating-point value to t when overflow does not occur, so no particular tie-breaking strategy is imposed. [PDF p. 5 (printed 688), Section 2.1]
The unit roundoff is u = (1/2) beta^(1-p), and u <= 1/2. [PDF p. 1 (printed 684), Introduction; PDF p. 5 (printed 688), equation (2.1)]

diag(f(i)) is the n by n diagonal matrix with diagonal entries f(1), ..., f(n). Thus diag((i+1)u) has diagonal entries 2u, 3u, ..., (n+1)u. [PDF p. 9 (printed 692), Section 4 notation paragraph; PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.4)]
The hats distinguish computed floating-point quantities from exact mathematical values. [PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Lemma 4.3 and Theorem 4.4; PDF p. 12 (printed 695), update formulas]

The matrix absolute values and inequalities in (4.4) are componentwise, as confirmed by the scalar entrywise estimates (4.5a)-(4.5b); juxtaposition |Rhat^T||Rhat| denotes ordinary matrix multiplication of the entrywise-absolute matrices. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equations (4.4)-(4.5b)]

For a symmetric positive-definite real matrix, the preceding paragraph defines the exact Cholesky factor as the unique upper-triangular R with positive diagonal and A = R^T R; Cholesky factorization means computing it with the conventional algorithm. [PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Section 4.3 opening paragraph]
implicit_context: The computed factor is the upper-triangular factor constructed one column at a time by the conventional method, not an arbitrary matrix satisfying a residual bound. [PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Section 4.3 opening; PDF p. 12 (printed 695), first proof paragraph]

The preceding positive-definite definition identifies the intended exact factor, but positive definiteness and existence of an exact positive-diagonal factor are not imported into the theorem's explicit hypotheses. [PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Section 4.3 opening and Theorem 4.4]
The result applies for any dimension n, including when (n+1)u is not less than one. [PDF p. 4 (printed 687), paragraph following equation (1.8)]

The arbitrary-order allowance concerns evaluation of the inner sums while the column progression j = 1, ..., n and the update dependencies remain those of the conventional algorithm. [PDF p. 3 (printed 686), order-of-evaluation definition; PDF p. 12 (printed 695), update formulas]
The proof obtains upper-triangular entry estimates and uses symmetry to cover the remaining entries. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equations (4.5a)-(4.5b) and closing sentence]
statement.algorithm_linkage: The theorem is tied to the conventional upper-triangular, column-by-column Cholesky algorithm. For j = 1, ..., n and i = 1, ..., j-1, it evaluates y_ij = (a_ij - sum_{k=1}^{i-1} Rhat_ki Rhat_kj) / Rhat_ii, and it evaluates y_jj = (a_jj - sum_{k=1}^{j-1} Rhat_kj^2)^(1/2). Rhat_ij and Rhat_jj are the resulting computed values, with arbitrary permitted evaluation order for the sums. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), conventional update formulas and paragraph preceding equations (4.5a)-(4.5b)]
numerical_model: Arithmetic uses a standard finite floating-point set with arbitrary radix beta >= 2 and precision p >= 1. [PDF p. 5 (printed 688), Section 2.1]
Operations are rounded to nearest, with no prescribed tie-breaking rule. [PDF p. 5 (printed 688), Section 2.1]
The unit roundoff is exactly u = (1/2) beta^(1-p). [PDF p. 1 (printed 684), Introduction; PDF p. 5 (printed 688), equation (2.1)]
The theorem covers every permitted order of evaluation of the inner sums. [PDF p. 3 (printed 686), order-of-evaluation paragraph; PDF p. 12 (printed 695), proof of Theorem 4.4]
No smallness condition such as (n+1)u < 1 is imposed. [PDF p. 4 (printed 687), paragraph following equation (1.8)]
error_notions: The result is a backward-error statement: the computed factor is the exact Cholesky-type factorization of the perturbed input A + DeltaA. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.4)]
The error bound is componentwise rather than normwise. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equations (4.4)-(4.5b)]
The componentwise envelope is measured against |Rhat^T||Rhat|, not against |A| and not against an exact Cholesky factor. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.4)]
The passage gives no forward-error estimate comparing Rhat with an exact factor R. [PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Theorem 4.4; PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.4)]

The input entries a_ij remain the exact data in the local residuals; DeltaA collects the discrepancy between those entries and the exact product of computed factor entries. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equations (4.5a)-(4.5b)]
norms: No vector or matrix norm occurs in Theorem 4.4; all displayed absolute values and inequalities are entrywise. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equations (4.4)-(4.5b)]

|Rhat^T||Rhat| is an ordinary matrix product after taking entrywise absolute values, not a Hadamard product or a norm. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.4) and its derivation from equations (4.5a)-(4.5b)]
constants_and_indexing: In diag((i+1)u), i ranges from 1 to n, so the row multipliers run from 2u through (n+1)u. [PDF p. 9 (printed 692), diag convention; PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.4)]

The first matrix bound scales row i of |Rhat^T||Rhat| by (i+1)u; the diagonal factor is on the left and must not be moved or replaced by a scalar in the sharper bound. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.4)]
The uniform bound uses the maximum diagonal multiplier, namely (n+1)u. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.4)]
For off-diagonal entry (i,j) with 1 <= i <= j-1, the local constant is iu and both residual and magnitude sums end at k = i. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.5a)]
For diagonal entry (j,j), the local constant is (j+1)u and both sums end at k = j. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.5b)]

The update formulas themselves use sums ending at i-1 for an off-diagonal entry and j-1 for a diagonal entry; the residual estimates include the newly computed kth endpoint. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), update formulas and equations (4.5a)-(4.5b)]
higher_order_terms: The bounds contain only constants linear in u: iu, (j+1)u, and (n+1)u. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equations (4.4)-(4.5b)]
There is no omitted O(u^2) remainder and no gamma_(n+1) denominator. [PDF p. 4 (printed 687), paragraph following equation (1.8); PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.4)]
The relation Rhat^T Rhat = A + DeltaA is exact; only the size of DeltaA is bounded. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.4)]
exceptional_values: The theorem excludes underflow and overflow during the floating-point computation. [PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Theorem 4.4]

The paper's underflow exclusion does not prohibit every subnormal value: underflow is defined as an inexact rounding of a real result lying in the subnormal range. [PDF p. 5 (printed 688), Section 2.1]

The scalar division lemma used in the proof requires a nonzero divisor, and the square-root lemma requires a nonnegative computed square-root argument. [PDF p. 10 (printed 693), Lemma 4.1; PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Lemma 4.3]

A and Rhat contain finite values because they belong to F. Infinities arise only as overflow results outside F, and NaNs are not explicitly modeled. [PDF p. 5 (printed 688), Section 2.1; PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Theorem 4.4]

undebatable_constraints: The input must be an n by n symmetric matrix with entries in F; replacing this by an arbitrary real matrix changes the theorem. [PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Theorem 4.4]

Positive definiteness must not be added as an explicit theorem hypothesis: the stated condition is symmetry together with successful completion of the conventional algorithm. [PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Section 4.3 opening and Theorem 4.4]

Rhat must be the computed output of the conventional upper-triangular Cholesky process, not an existentially chosen approximate factor. [PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Section 4.3; PDF p. 12 (printed 695), update formulas]
The exact product is Rhat^T Rhat, in that order, and the backward relation is Rhat^T Rhat = A + DeltaA. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.4)]
Both parts of the bound must be preserved: the sharper row-scaled bound with diag((i+1)u) and the coarser bound with (n+1)u. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.4)]
The bounds are componentwise and use the ordinary matrix product |Rhat^T||Rhat|; they are not norm bounds. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equations (4.4)-(4.5b)]
The index offset is +1: the diagonal coefficient is (j+1)u and the global coefficient is (n+1)u, while the off-diagonal local coefficient is iu. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equations (4.4)-(4.5b)]

The result assumes round-to-nearest arithmetic, permits arbitrary tie-breaking and inner-sum evaluation order, and excludes underflow and overflow. [PDF p. 4 (printed 687), paragraph following equation (1.8); PDF p. 5 (printed 688), Section 2.1; PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Theorem 4.4]
No condition such as (n+1)u < 1 and no O(u^2) term may be introduced. [PDF p. 4 (printed 687), paragraph following equation (1.8); PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.4)]

ambiguities.issue: The phrase runs to completion is not reduced to explicit algebraic side conditions.
ambiguities.evidence: The theorem uses runs to completion without defining it locally; the proof divides by Rhat_ii, Lemma 4.1 requires a nonzero divisor, and Lemma 4.3 requires a nonnegative computed square-root argument. [PDF p. 10 (printed 693), Lemma 4.1; PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Lemma 4.3 and Theorem 4.4; PDF p. 12 (printed 695), update formulas]
ambiguities.impact: A formal contract should retain an execution-success condition or define the algorithmic validity conditions explicitly. It should not silently replace successful completion by positive definiteness, and the passage does not resolve whether a zero final diagonal counts as completion.

ambiguities.issue: DeltaA is introduced without an explicit binder or scalar type.
ambiguities.evidence: Equation (4.4) directly writes Rhat^T Rhat = A + DeltaA and bounds DeltaA, but does not state DeltaA belongs to F^(n by n) or R^(n by n). [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.4)]
ambiguities.impact: The natural reading is the exact residual DeltaA = Rhat^T Rhat - A in real arithmetic; requiring DeltaA itself to have floating-point entries would add an unsupported condition.

ambiguities.issue: The matrix absolute-value convention is not separately defined in the inspected passage.
ambiguities.evidence: Equation (4.4) uses matrix bars and inequalities, while equations (4.5a)-(4.5b) provide scalar entrywise inequalities from which it is derived. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equations (4.4)-(4.5b)]
ambiguities.impact: The derivation makes the componentwise interpretation clear, but a formalization must encode entrywise absolute values and order rather than select a matrix norm.

ambiguities.issue: Strict positivity of the computed diagonal is not stated as a theorem conclusion.
ambiguities.evidence: The preceding exact-factor definition gives positive diagonal entries for a symmetric positive-definite input, whereas Theorem 4.4 assumes only symmetry and successful completion; the computed diagonal is produced by a rounded square root. [PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Section 4.3 opening and Theorem 4.4; PDF p. 12 (printed 695), diagonal update formula]
ambiguities.impact: Strict positivity of every computed diagonal entry must not be added unless it follows from a separately specified execution-success semantics.

ambiguities.evidence: The paper specifies the conventional quotient and square-root update formulas and allows arbitrary binary-tree orders for their sums, but it does not state that fused multiply-add evaluations are included. [PDF p. 3 (printed 686), order-of-evaluation paragraph; PDF p. 12 (printed 695), update formulas]
ambiguities.impact: The contract covers the stated standard-operation evaluation model and arbitrary summation order; extending it to an FMA-based Cholesky variant would require an additional argument.

contract_plain_english: For any symmetric finite floating-point matrix A, run the conventional upper-triangular, column-by-column Cholesky algorithm in round-to-nearest arithmetic. Assume that the execution completes and that no underflow or overflow occurs; inner sums may use any permitted evaluation order. [PDF p. 5 (printed 688), Sections 2.1-2.2; PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Theorem 4.4; PDF p. 12 (printed 695), update formulas] The computed factor Rhat then exactly factors a perturbed input: Rhat^T Rhat = A + DeltaA, with the componentwise bounds |DeltaA| <= diag((i+1)u)|Rhat^T||Rhat| <= (n+1)u|Rhat^T||Rhat|, where i ranges from 1 to n. [PDF p. 9 (printed 692), diag convention; PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equation (4.4)] The proof's local constants are iu off the diagonal and (j+1)u on the diagonal. [PDF p. 12 (printed 695), equations (4.5a)-(4.5b)] Positive definiteness is not required by the theorem, there is no condition (n+1)u < 1, and no O(u^2) term is omitted. [PDF p. 4 (printed 687), paragraph following equation (1.8); PDF p. 11 (printed 694), Theorem 4.4]
